newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo's WTO admission hinges on political factors.
newsitem.headline: Yugo's WTO admission hinges on political factors.

text.p: An influential Belgrade trade body said on Thursday it did not believe Yugoslavia had the political will to become a member of the World Trade Organisation in the near term.

"We have lost all illusions Yugoslavia can become a member of the WTO on the basis of earlier GATT membership," Radovan Kovacevic, director of the Institute for Foreign Trade told Reuters in an interview.

Yugoslavia was suspended from international trade organisations, including the WTO's forerunner GATT (General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade) in 1992 when the U.N. imposed sanctions on Belgrade for its role in the Bosnia war.
Although WTO membership is seen as crucial for the Yugoslav economy's reintegration in world markets, the government appears reluctant to move in that direction, analysts said.
Full liberalisation of trade, as WTO membership implies, would not give domestic industry a chance to get back on its feet after years of crippling sanctions.
"The government probably feels the moment is not politically opportune to formally submit a request," the institute's Zivadin Jevtic told Reuters.
Recent cuts in import duties met with fierce opposition from domestic producers who said cheap imports would stifle local industry.
"But we must accept trade liberalisation and slowly begin forgetting quotas and export-import permits," Kovacevic said.
Yugoslavia had initially planned to ask for developing nation status, which would give it a longer period to adjust and reduce customs tariffs, but talks have yet to begin.
Kovacevic suggested Yugoslavia should show the same inventiveness in conceiving some form of protection for its economy as the United States and certain western European countries have done.
An outer wall of sanctions, imposed by Washington, still barred the country from access to international organisations, including the International Montetary Fund (IMF).
Formally, the WTO could resist Yugoslav membership because it was not a member of the United Nations.
"But a green light from Washington is more important," Kovacevic said.

Yugoslav Foreign Trade minister Borislav Vukovic said last week Yugoslavia had fulfilled more than 90 percent of conditions for admission, and was prepared to incorporate all WTO requirements in its legislation.

"Yugoslavia's return to the WTO depends on when we will take our place in the United Nations and the IMF, and return to them depends on international factors who are not supportive," Vukovic told state news agency Tanjug.
